Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

issues.explanation: Global mistrust of other people is a weak fit with a primary trauma of life-threatening illness in the absence of any interpersonal betrayal, assault, or persecution content elsewhere in the profile. The rest of the appraisals are centered on bodily threat and fear of losing control, making this item comparatively incoherent.

vignette:
Two years ago, on a busy Saturday afternoon, Amir nicked his thumb with a pair of thinning shears. The cut was small, barely bleeding, and he rinsed it under the sink before finishing his last client. Within forty-eight hours he was in the emergency room with a skyrocketing fever, his hand swollen and streaked with red. The infection had entered his bloodstream. What followed was a blur of ICU stays, two surgical debridements, and a week on a ventilator. He remembers very little of that week except the smell—a sharp, chemical antiseptic that seemed to be everywhere—and a grinding, burning pain deep in his abdomen where the infection had settled. When he finally woke, the doctors told him he had been hours from death.

Recovery was slow. Amir went back to work after three months, but something had shifted. He found himself avoiding the medical dramas his coworkers sometimes played on the salon TV. Worse was the first time a client handed him a photo of their new grandchild—a snapshot taken in a hospital waiting room. The image of fluorescent lights and beige curtains hit him like a wave, and his chest tightened. His hands began to shake, and that antiseptic smell returned, vivid and nauseating, even though nothing in the salon smelled that way. The memory of the pain in his abdomen flared for a moment, as real as the original. That visceral recollection made him begin to scan his body for any small ache or sensation, turning ordinary bodily signals into potential triggers he had never noticed before. That afternoon he had to excuse himself to the back room. The experience convinced him that his body was fundamentally untrustworthy—that it could betray him without warning. That conviction—that his own body was a hidden enemy—kept dragging him back into the ICU memory, forcing him to relive the smell and the burning pain as if his belief had unlocked the door to the past. From then on, he began to monitor any small physical sensation obsessively: a twinge in his gut, a scratch on his arm, the beat of his heart. Every such sensation felt like a signal that the illness was coming back. He started to believe he was going crazy—why else would a photo make him smell things that weren't there?

The nightmares started about a month after the photo incident. He would wake drenched in sweat, his heart hammering, the full emotional terror of the ICU washing over him without any clear image attached. It was just pure, formless dread, as if the event were happening again in his body even though his mind was awake. Those nights left him exhausted and jumpy the next day. A routine physical exam for his hairdresser's license became unbearable: when the doctor pressed on his abdomen, Amir went rigid, his whole body screaming danger, and the pain memory surged back so strongly he nearly cried out. He told himself he was overreacting, that his body was safe now, but he could not shake the feeling that it was an enemy hiding inside his skin.

At the salon, he became hypervigilant. Any cut, any splash of disinfectant, any client who talked about a hospital visit sent him into a low-level panic. He started avoiding social media feeds that might contain medical content. The belief that his body was unreliable made him scan his own reactions constantly, which in turn sharpened his sensitivity to even neutral triggers. When he felt that constant physical tension—the knot in his stomach, the tightness in his shoulders—it often dragged the memory back into focus, and he would relive the smell and pain all over again. The loop tightened: a nightmare triggered a day of scanning, scanning made him notice a tiny ache, the ache brought back the full memory, and the memory convinced him he was going crazy, which made his body even more alert.

What finally brought him to seek help was an incident last week. A regular client brought in a photo from her own mother's recent surgery. Before Amir could look away, he saw the image, and within seconds his entire body was flooded with fear. His hands trembled so badly he had to set down his comb. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink, fighting the urge to flee the salon entirely. That was the moment he realized he could not keep going this way—that his life was shrinking around a fear he could no longer explain away. He is terrified that talking about the event will make it worse, but he is equally afraid that if he does not find a way out, he will lose his business, his friendships, and whatever peace he has left.
